note: Two disciples, Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai and Rabbi Yehuda, son of converts, took leave of their teacher Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai in the evening and came back to take leave again in the morning, explaining that he had taught them a disciple who stays the night in the same city must do so twice. Impressed, Rabbi Shimon sent his son to them for a blessing. The son found them working through contradictions between verses; when they noticed him, they wished on him that he sow and not reap, bring in and not take out, that his house be destroyed, and that he not see a new year. He came home hurt, but his father told him these were all blessings in disguise, and began decoding them: he would have sons and they would not die, bring in brides for them, and his daughters' husbands would not die.
why: The Gemara has been reading the verses about Solomon dedicating the Temple and sending the people home; the disciples draw their practice of a second farewell from those very verses.

people.name: Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai
people.about: A disciple of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai who, with his study partner, gave the puzzling blessing.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda, son of converts
people.about: Rabbi Yonatan's study partner, also a disciple of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: The teacher of the two disciples; he sends his son to them and then explains their words.

terms.meaning: A formal farewell a student gives his teacher before departing. The disciples hold that if a student stays overnight in the city afterward, he must take leave again.
A commandment or religious duty from the Torah.

flag: The story stops partway through Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's explanation: the decoding of the last three blessings (house and lodging, the table, the new year) falls in the segments after it.
